batchName: Empire: Augustus and the Principate (27 BC-AD 14) - Hard Batch 1
chapterName: Empire: Augustus and the Principate (27 BC-AD 14)

questions.question: Which statement best describes marble's place in Augustan Rome?
options: It was reserved for temples alone
It was banned in favour of brick
It was first brought to Rome by Augustus
It became standard under Julius Caesar
It was used only for the Senate house
Used before, it only became standard under Augustus
questions.explanation: Marble was not new, but only under Augustus did it become a standard building material, which gave substance to his traditional boast.
questions.sourceQuote: Marble had been used before, but only under Augustus did it become a standard building material.

questions.question: Behind Augustus's claim to rule by personal prestige, which hard facts underpinned his power? (select all that apply)
options: A network of clients and supporters
Election as dictator for life
An alliance with the Parthian king
Legal powers voted by Senate and people
An enormous private fortune
A hereditary royal title
questions.explanation: Augustus said he ruled by auctoritas rather than by office, but his power rested on legal powers, his fortune and his network of clients and supporters.
questions.sourceQuote: Behind the polite words stood three hard facts: legal powers voted by Senate and people, an enormous private fortune, and a vast network of clients and supporters bound to him by favours.

questions.question: Writing in 1939, how did a famous British historian portray the young Octavian's faction?
options: As God-sent peacemakers
As something like a crime gang
As a genuine partnership with the Senate
As a band of reluctant rulers
As defenders of the Republic
As heirs of Greek philosophy
questions.explanation: Writing as fascist dictators borrowed Roman imagery, he called Octavian "sickly and sinister". More recent writers say comparisons with modern tyrants are misleading.
questions.sourceQuote: A famous British historian, writing in 1939 as fascist dictators borrowed Roman imagery, painted the young Octavian as "sickly and sinister" and his faction as something like a crime gang.

questions.question: After the civil wars, to how many legions did Augustus reduce the Roman army?
questions.explanation: He cut the army from about 60 legions to 28, some 170,000 professional soldiers backed by non-citizen auxiliaries. In AD 6 he set up a military treasury to pay them.
questions.sourceQuote: After the civil wars he cut the army from about 60 legions to 28, some 170,000 professional soldiers, backed by auxiliary units of non-citizens.

questions.question: In 32 BC, on whom did the Senate formally declare war?
options: Antony and the queen jointly
The Egyptian queen
The renegade admiral
The Parthian king
Mark Antony personally
The third triumvir
questions.explanation: War was declared on the Egyptian queen, not on Antony. A year after Actium, Antony and the queen both took their own lives.
questions.sourceQuote: In 32 BC the Senate declared war on the Egyptian queen.

questions.question: Which sequence correctly orders the deaths that disrupted Augustus's plans for an heir?
options: His nephew, then Gaius and Lucius, then Agrippa
Gaius and Lucius, then his nephew, then Agrippa
His nephew, then Agrippa, then Gaius and Lucius
Agrippa, then his nephew, then Gaius and Lucius
Agrippa, then Gaius and Lucius, then his nephew
Gaius and Lucius, then Agrippa, then his nephew
questions.explanation: His nephew died in 23 BC, Agrippa in 12 BC, and Gaius and Lucius in AD 2 and AD 4. That left Tiberius as heir.
questions.sourceQuote: Augustus adopted their sons Gaius and Lucius, but Agrippa died in 12 BC, and both boys died young, in AD 2 and AD 4.

questions.question: Where and when did Antony and Octavian defeat the armies of Caesar's assassins?
options: Philippi in Macedonia, 44 BC
Mutina in northern Italy, 43 BC
Philippi in Macedonia, 42 BC
Actium in western Greece, 31 BC
Alexandria in Egypt, 30 BC
Pharsalus in Thessaly, 48 BC
questions.explanation: The assassins were crushed at Philippi in northern Greece in 42 BC. Afterwards the victors carved up the Roman world.
questions.sourceQuote: In 42 BC Antony and Octavian crushed the assassins' armies at Philippi in Macedonia, in northern Greece.

questions.question: Which qualities of Augustus did the golden shield in the Senate house praise? (select all that apply)
options: Eloquence
Courage
Mercy
Wealth
Piety
Justice
questions.explanation: Augustus refused a crown or sceptre, but accepted a golden shield praising his courage, piety, mercy and justice.
questions.sourceQuote: He refused a crown or sceptre, but a golden shield in the Senate house praised his courage, piety, mercy and justice.

questions.question: Near Kalkriese, what trapped the Roman survivors of the ambush in AD 9?
options: A narrow gap between a hill and a bog, behind a hidden wall
A flooded river crossing guarded by archers
A mountain pass blocked by fallen trees
A burning forest surrounding their camp
A Roman fort betrayed from within
A ravine sealed off by Germanic cavalry
questions.explanation: The gap was only about 100 metres wide, behind a hidden earthen wall. The Roman column had been strung out over 15 to 20 km.
questions.sourceQuote: Near Kalkriese, in northern Germany, the survivors were trapped in a gap only about 100 metres (330 feet) wide between a hill and a bog, behind a hidden earthen wall.

questions.question: By AD 13, how many times had Augustus's troops hailed him as victorious general (imperator)?
questions.explanation: He was hailed imperator 21 times. Augustus called his peace one "born of victories".
questions.sourceQuote: By AD 13 his troops had hailed him as victorious general (*imperator*) 21 times.
